Family

Caring for an older relative without losing yourself

Caring for a dependent parent is an act of love and also a burden. Looking after the carer is not selfish.

Much of the care for dependent older people is provided by relatives, often middle-aged women. Helping a mother or father with dementia, limited mobility or a chronic illness can bring meaning and closeness, but it is also exhausting.

The cost of caring

A 2003 review by Martin Pinquart and Silvia Sörensen pooled more than two hundred studies and found that carers have more stress and depressive symptoms, and slightly worse physical health, than non-carers. The burden is greater when the person cared for has behavioural problems, as in some dementias, and when the carer has little support.

It is common to feel contradictory emotions: love, helplessness, guilt at not managing everything, anger and then guilt about the anger. All are normal.

What usually helps

  • Ask for and accept help from other relatives, even if they do not do it "as well".
  • Find out about resources: day centres, home help, short respite stays and dependency benefits. Social services and your health centre can advise.
  • Keep some time for yourself each week, however little.
  • Join carers' support groups, which reduce isolation.
  • Look after your own health: sleep, eat and attend your check-ups.
If you notice constant exhaustion, irritability, sadness or feel overwhelmed, tell your GP. Looking after yourself is also part of caring.

References

  1. Pinquart, M. y Sörensen, S. (2003). Differences between caregivers and noncaregivers in psychological health and physical health: a meta-analysis. Psychology and Aging, 18(2), 250–267.
  2. IMSERSO. Cuidar a quien cuida. Ministerio de Derechos Sociales.
